label.working: Both tripeptides share the exact same amino acid composition and molecular mass, joined by peptide bonds. Because sequence determines the spatial arrangement and chemical environment of the R-groups, changing the sequence alters the 3D shape and chemical presentation, affecting antibody-binding specificity.

The two forms of carvone are enantiomers with the same chemical formula and molecular mass, differing only in their three-dimensional spatial orientation. Protein receptors have specific, complementary binding sites whose interactions depend on 3D shape, meaning only the complementary stereoisomer fits effectively.

Both glucose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the identical formula C6H12O6 but different 3D stereochemistry. Membrane transport proteins (permeases) exhibit ligand-binding specificity determined by molecular shape and chemical complementarity; thus, the distinct orientation of hydroxyl groups means glucose fits the transporter's binding site more effectively than galactose.

Leucine has a nonpolar, hydrophobic R group. Placing hydrophobic residues on the exterior of a soluble protein in an aqueous environment leads to aggregation because the nonpolar side chains associate with each other via hydrophobic interactions to minimize contact with water.

Normally, negatively charged aspartate and positively charged lysine form an attractive ionic interaction at the dimer interface (quaternary structure). Replacing lysine with glutamate places two negatively charged side chains in close proximity, causing electrostatic repulsion and preventing stable dimer formation.

Valine is nonpolar and resides favorably in the hydrophobic core. Aspartate has a charged, hydrophilic side chain. Placing a charged group into a nonpolar interior causes unfavorable energetics and disrupts tertiary folding, reducing stability and activity. A, B, and D make scientifically incorrect statements about protein structure.

Both tripeptides contain the same three amino acids joined by the same peptide bonds, so composition, mass, and linkage type are identical. The order differs, so the R groups and overall three-dimensional arrangement differ, affecting fit with antibody. A, C, and D are false.

Galactose and glucose are isomers: same atoms, different spatial arrangement, hence different 3D shapes. A transport protein's binding site is specific to substrate shape, so glucose fits better than galactose and is imported faster. Choices A, C, and D are factually incorrect.

Serine is polar and uncharged; leucine is nonpolar and hydrophobic. Replacing a surface serine with leucine exposes hydrophobic side chains to water. To avoid water, nonpolar side chains on separate protein molecules associate via hydrophobic interactions, causing aggregation. Peptide bonds, hydrogen bonding to water, and ionic attraction are not involved.

Cell 1 lacks membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus (features defining prokaryotes), while Cell 2 contains a nucleus, chloroplasts, and mitochondria (features defining eukaryotes). Thus, C is directly supported.

The wild-type dimer interface is stabilized by an ionic attraction between negatively charged Asp40 and positively charged Lys112. Replacing Lys112 with negatively charged glutamate removes that attraction and places two like charges next to each other, causing repulsion and destabilizing the dimer. B, C, and D misstate peptide bonds, glutamate polarity, and disulfide bond chemistry.

Cell 1 has circular DNA and lacks membrane-bound organelles, defining features of prokaryotes. Cell 2 has a nucleus, mitochondria, and eukaryotic organelles, defining it as eukaryotic. Although Cell 1 is unusually large and Cell 2 is relatively small, cellular classification is determined by internal structural organization and compartmentalization, not diameter.

Cell 1 has features typical of a photosynthetic prokaryote (cyanobacterium): circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall, and no membrane-bound organelles. Cell 2 contains a nucleus, chloroplasts, and 80S ribosomes, indicating it is eukaryotic. Therefore, choice A is directly supported.

Valine is nonpolar and buried in the hydrophobic interior. Aspartate is charged; placing a charged side chain among nonpolar groups is energetically unfavorable, destabilizing the folded tertiary structure. A is wrong because stability decreases; B is wrong because aspartate can form peptide bonds; D is wrong because primary structure determines folding.

The potato core placed in 0.6 M sucrose lost mass because the surrounding solution was hypertonic (lower water potential), causing net movement of water out of the plant cells via osmosis. The loss of water reduced intracellular volume and turgor pressure, leading to flaccid (limp) tissue.

The stem states the two forms have identical atoms and bonds but are mirror images, so formulas and masses are identical, eliminating A and C; carvone is a small molecule, not a protein (B). Receptor-ligand binding depends on three-dimensional shape complementarity, so only the mirror-image form that fits the binding site binds strongly.

0.6 M sucrose is hypertonic to the potato cells, so water moves by osmosis from the cells into the solution. This lowers turgor pressure and makes the tissue limp. Distilled water is hypotonic, so water enters and cells become firm.

The rigid plant cell wall exerts turgor pressure to counteract inward osmotic water flow in a hypotonic environment (distilled water), preventing cell lysis. When the wall is enzymatically digested to yield protoplasts, only the fragile plasma membrane remains; water continues to enter by osmosis until the membrane lyses and the cell bursts.

Cell 1 has circular DNA free in cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, so it is prokaryotic. Cell 2 has a nucleus, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes, and a chitin wall, so it is eukaryotic (fungal). Thus internal structure, not size, separates the two cells.

A salty solution creates a hypertonic external environment with lower water potential. Water moves out of the plant cells via osmosis, resulting in plasmolysis (plasma membrane shrinking away from the cell wall), loss of turgor pressure, and wilting.

Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires specific ligand-receptor binding at the cell surface to trigger vesicle formation. Without functional transferrin receptors on the plasma membrane, transferrin cannot bind, preventing its internalization; thus, it stays in the bloodstream and the cells become iron-deficient.

Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have them. Cell 1 has a nucleoid and no membrane-bound organelles, while Cell 2 has a nucleus, chloroplasts, and mitochondria. Thus C is directly supported. A, B, and D are false because flagella and cell walls occur in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

Since the toxin prevents vesicle fusion without affecting synthesis, insulin continues to be produced and packaged into vesicles, accumulating inside the cell. Without exocytosis, insulin is not released into the bloodstream, preventing glucose uptake and leaving blood glucose levels elevated.

A very salty external solution is hypertonic to the leaf cells. Water moves by osmosis from higher water potential inside the cells to lower water potential outside, so the protoplast loses volume, pulls away from the cell wall, and turgor pressure drops. Loss of turgor causes wilting. A, B, and D incorrectly involve salt entry, cell wall dissolution, or water influx.

The prompt states that LDL still binds to receptors, but inward membrane folding and pinching off (endocytosis) are inhibited. Because LDL is a large macromolecular complex, it cannot diffuse across the lipid bilayer. Thus, LDL remains at the cell surface without entering, causing blood LDL concentrations to rise.

Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water enters by osmosis in both intact cells and protoplasts. In intact cells the rigid cellulose wall resists expansion, creating turgor pressure; protoplasts lack that wall, so the plasma membrane swells until it ruptures. A and D misstate membrane loss/water movement; B incorrectly calls the cytoplasm isotonic.

Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires surface transferrin receptors to bind transferrin and trigger vesicle uptake. Without functional receptors, transferrin cannot be internalized, so iron delivery to developing red blood cells decreases. Large proteins cannot cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion, ruling out B.

An internal osmolarity of 280 mOsm/L means an isotonic solution is ~280 mOsm/L (P, no shape change). Shrinking (crenation) occurs in a hypertonic solution with higher osmolarity, so Q > 280 mOsm/L (600 mOsm/L). Swelling and lysis occur in a hypotonic solution with lower osmolarity, so R < 280 mOsm/L (50 mOsm/L).

Exocytosis is blocked, so vesicles cannot fuse with the membrane and release insulin. Since insulin synthesis is unaffected, insulin accumulates inside undelivered vesicles and blood glucose remains elevated. The other choices contradict the described block, ignore insulin's polarity, or wrongly claim synthesis stops.

Solution A (150 mOsm/L) is hypotonic to the cell (300 mOsm/L), so water enters down its water potential gradient, causing swelling/lysis. Solution B (300 mOsm/L) is isotonic, resulting in no net volume change. Solution C (450 mOsm/L) is hypertonic, drawing water out and causing the cell to shrink.

Water moves from lower osmolarity (hypotonic) to higher osmolarity (hypertonic). Cell swelling (+25% in Solution 1) indicates the lowest osmolarity. No change (0% in Solution 3) indicates isotonicity. Shrinkage (-18% in Solution 2, -30% in Solution 4) indicates progressively higher external osmolarities. Thus, lowest to highest is 1, 3, 2, 4.

P normal shape means the solution is approximately isotonic to the cytoplasm, about 280 mOsm/L. Q shrank/wrinkled means water left the cells, so Q is hypertonic (>280). R swelled and burst means water entered, so R is hypotonic (<280). Thus P=280, Q=600, R=50.

Receptor-mediated endocytosis internalizes bound LDL by membrane invagination and vesicle pinching off. If pinching off is blocked after binding, LDL remains bound at the cell surface and is not cleared from blood, raising blood LDL. A, B, and D contradict the described binding/normal mechanism.

Proteins destined for secretion follow the endomembrane pathway: rough ER to Golgi to secretory vesicles to plasma membrane fusion (exocytosis). Inhibiting vesicle fusion blocks the final export step without instantly halting upstream synthesis, causing the protein to accumulate inside intracellular vesicles and markedly reducing secretion.

Water moves by osmosis from lower to higher osmolarity. Solution A (150 mOsm/L) is hypotonic to the cytoplasm (300 mOsm/L), so cells swell and may lyse. Solution B (300 mOsm/L) is isotonic, so no net volume change. Solution C (450 mOsm/L) is hypertonic, so cells lose water and shrink.

Ribosomes on the rough ER still synthesize hydrolytic enzymes because synthesis is unaffected. However, if the Golgi complex cannot package them into transport vesicles to form or replenish lysosomes, functional hydrolytic enzymes will fail to reach the lysosomes, resulting in decreased digestion and accumulation of worn-out cellular components.

The rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi complex are part of the endomembrane system responsible for synthesizing, processing, and packaging proteins destined for secretion. Since Cell W secretes large amounts of a protein hormone, it requires the most extensive rough ER and Golgi complex.

The double membrane structure—specifically the outer membrane resembling the eukaryotic host's vacuolar/plasma membrane and the inner membrane resembling the engulfed bacterial membrane—specifically demonstrates the engulfment/uptake mechanism of endosymbiosis, whereas choices A, B, and C contain scientifically incorrect claims.

Antibody is a secreted protein synthesized on rough ER, modified in the Golgi, and packaged into vesicles. If Golgi-derived vesicles cannot fuse with the plasma membrane, exocytosis is blocked, so antibody is still produced and traffics into Golgi/vesicles but accumulates inside the cell with little secretion.

Ribosomes on the rough ER synthesize lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes, and the Golgi complex packages and sorts them into vesicles for lysosomes. Blocking only Golgi packaging leaves synthesis intact, so enzymes do not reach lysosomes. Worn-out components are digested less and accumulate.

Cells swell in hypotonic (low-osmolarity) solutions and shrink in hypertonic (high-osmolarity) solutions; no volume change indicates isotonic. Thus +25% is lowest osmolarity, then 0%, then -18%, then -30%, giving Solution 1, Solution 3, Solution 2, Solution 4.

Protein-secreting cells need abundant rough ER and Golgi. Cell W secretes large amounts of a protein hormone, so it is the correct choice. Steroid/lipid synthesis is smooth ER, fat storage and contraction do not indicate extensive rough ER/Golgi.

The proposal posits an endosymbiotic origin from a bacterium. Molecular sequence comparison showing high similarity between the organelle's DNA and free-living photosynthetic bacteria provides direct phylogenetic evidence of bacterial ancestry, distinguishing it from an autogenous eukaryotic origin. The other options describe universal cellular features that do not demonstrate bacterial lineage.

According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria descended from engulfed aerobic bacteria and thus retain bacterial-like (70S) ribosomes. Since antibiotic Q specifically inhibits 70S ribosomes without affecting eukaryotic 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, treatment will inhibit protein synthesis inside mitochondria while sparing cytoplasmic translation.

The outer surface of the transmembrane region contacts the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, requiring nonpolar R groups. The interior pore accommodates hydrophilic, hydrated ions, requiring polar or charged R groups.

The inner membrane resembling a bacterial plasma membrane and the outer membrane resembling the host indicate an ancestral prokaryote was engulfed and retained within a host-derived membrane. The other options overstate or misinterpret DNA, ribosome, or division evidence, which merely show prokaryote-like features, not the uptake event.

High-salt solutions disrupt ionic and polar interactions without disrupting the hydrophobic bilayer, releasing peripheral membrane proteins. Since Protein Q has mostly polar and charged surface R groups, it interacts with the hydrophilic heads of phospholipids or surface proteins on the membrane exterior.

The nonpolar R groups interact stably with the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer, while hydrophilic (polar) segments interact with the aqueous cytoplasm and extracellular fluid. Seven hydrophobic segments of ~20 amino acids indicate a seven-transmembrane integral protein requiring detergent to extract, making D the only supported model.

Mitochondria likely originated from engulfed bacteria, so their ribosomes should resemble bacterial 70S ribosomes. Antibiotic Q inhibits 70S but not 80S ribosomes, so mitochondrial protein synthesis would be inhibited while cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes continue.

Transmembrane proteins span the hydrophobic bilayer. R groups facing the phospholipid tails must be nonpolar/hydrophobic, while R groups lining an ion- and water-filled pore must be polar/hydrophilic to interact with ions and water. Thus D is correct; A, B, and C reverse or omit this pattern.

Cell 2 has a nucleus and chloroplasts, so it is eukaryotic. Cell 1 has a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and photosynthetic membranes continuous with the plasma membrane rather than chloroplasts; prokaryotes can photosynthesize, so Cell 1 is prokaryotic. Option A is directly supported. Other choices make false claims about photosynthesis or membranes.

Insulin triggers GLUT4 vesicle fusion, increasing membrane transporters. Since glucose is polar, it cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer directly and moves down its concentration gradient without ATP via facilitated diffusion through GLUT4, decreasing blood glucose levels. C correctly traces this sequence.

With normal CFTR, chloride channels in the membrane allow Cl⁻ to flow out into the airway surface liquid. This increases solute concentration in the extracellular liquid layer, causing water to follow by osmosis from the cells into the layer, keeping it well hydrated and the mucus thin.

Small uncharged polar molecules like water can cross the phospholipid bilayer directly via simple diffusion, but at a much slower rate. Aquaporins facilitate rapid transport of large amounts of water. Without aquaporins, water still enters down its osmotic gradient across the membrane bilayer, just more slowly, delaying lysis.

Endosymbiosis predicts the organelle retains bacterial genetic signatures. DNA sequence similarity to free-living photosynthetic bacteria, rather than to nuclear DNA, is direct molecular evidence of bacterial ancestry. Ribosomes, cytoplasmic location, and phospholipids are universal features and do not specifically support engulfment, so B is strongest.

Nonpolar R groups are hydrophobic, so they would localize in the membrane interior; polar regions would face aqueous environments. Being removable only by dissolving the lipid bilayer with detergent indicates an integral membrane protein embedded in the bilayer. The seven nonpolar stretches of about 20 amino acids each suggest multiple transmembrane segments, so Protein T crosses the bilayer several times.

The stem states GLUT4 insertion increases glucose channels and glucose enters down its concentration gradient without ATP. That describes facilitated diffusion, not simple diffusion through phospholipids or active pumping. Only C correctly links insulin, GLUT4 vesicle fusion, more channels, facilitated diffusion into muscle cells, and falling blood glucose.

AQP1 is an aquaporin, a facilitated-diffusion water channel; it does not use ATP. Without it, water still crosses the phospholipid bilayer slowly, so lysis is delayed, not prevented. Choice C is ruled out because the stem states internal osmolarities are identical in both groups.

High salt releases only surface-associated proteins by disrupting polar/ionic interactions; bilayer remains. Polar/charged surface R groups imply hydrophilic interactions with phospholipid heads or other membrane proteins, not hydrophobic tails. Thus B. A and D contradict polarity/water; C would remain embedded and require nonpolar membrane contact.

In normal CFTR, chloride exits through the channel into the airway liquid, raising its solute concentration. Osmosis then moves water from the cells into that liquid layer, keeping mucus thin. Option C states this correctly. A reverses water/chloride roles; B and D have chloride direction wrong.
